title: Update on my AI-made sci-fi game: one concept image in, a walkable level out. Here's the whole pipeline
author: Exciting-Pool5495
selftext:
Hey everyone! Last time I shared the loop that nudges a scene in **Krakatoa Circle 2** toward a painting. Since then I've been building something bigger: one pipeline that takes a single reference image and builds the level from it. That means the room, every object in it, the lights, and a check that a player can actually walk around.

Here is the first full scene it has built, the bedroom of Asha, the main character. The reference is on the left. The level is on the right, seen from the same camera:

https://i.redd.it/mkloucsxd72i1.jpeg

It isn't a match yet, and I'll get to what's still off. But nothing in the right-hand picture was placed by hand. Here's how it works today.

**The pipeline at a glance**

Two lanes run side by side. One finds and builds every object. The other builds the room itself. Then they're put together, lit and checked.

https://i.redd.it/69hipfo4e72i1.jpeg

**Step 1: Find everything in the picture**

1. A vision model lists everything it can see in the whole picture.
2. SAM 3 cuts an outline for each thing. The vision model then looks at every outline, and the wrong ones are cut again.
3. Everything found so far is greyed out and the vision model is asked what is still there. This repeats until a pass finds nothing new.

On the bedroom it found 21 things on the first look, 14 more on the second pass and 1 on the third. The fourth pass found nothing, so it stopped. It then found 6 built parts of the room itself (wall ribs, the door frame, a light beside the door).

https://i.redd.it/aermcebae72i1.jpeg

**Step 2: Draw each object again, by itself**

In the reference, most objects are half hidden, cut off by the frame, or lit by the room. So each one is cropped out and ChatGPT draws it again: alone, whole, on a transparent background, in a three-quarter view from a little above, so its front, one side and its top are all visible. It fills in what the picture hides and leaves out anything that gets its own model (the jacket hanging on the lockers, for example).

https://i.redd.it/uo498cbde72i1.jpeg

**Step 3: Turn each picture into a 3D model with Tripo**

This is the step Tripo does. Each clean picture goes to Tripo's image-to-3D API and comes back as a textured model (GLB). It's three calls per object:

1. **Upload the picture:** `POST /v3/files` returns a `file_token`.
2. **Start the job:** `POST /v3/generation/image-to-model` returns a `task_id`.
3. **Wait and download:** poll `GET /v3/tasks/{task_id}` until the status is `success`, then download `output.model_url` right away. The link expires after five minutes.

The request for a piece of furniture looks like this:

    POST https://openapi.tripo3d.ai/v3/generation/image-to-model
    Authorization: Bearer $TRIPO_API_KEY
    
    {
      "input": "<file_token>",
      "model": "v3.1-20260211",
      "texture": true,
      "pbr": true,
      "texture_quality": "detailed"
    }

The settings that matter for a pipeline like this:

* `pbr`: the model comes with base colour, metallic, roughness and normal maps, so the level's own lamps light it.
* `delight`: removes lighting that is baked into the picture. I want the material, not the room's warm lamp painted onto it.
* `face_limit`: caps the triangle count. Furniture gets a bigger budget than a mug.
* The P series models (`P1-20260311`, `P2-20260801`): low-poly output with clean topology, which suits small props.
* `model_seed` and `texture_seed`: the same picture and seed give the same model, so a rebuild doesn't reshuffle the scene.
* I leave `auto_size` off. The pipeline sizes each model from the depth of the reference instead.

Every object is its own job, so a whole scene runs in parallel. The Tripo CLI has a batch mode that fits this well: one manifest with a row per object, then `tripo batch run scene.yaml --concurrency 4`. It can be resumed, and finished rows are skipped on a re-run. For a single object it's `tripo make lockers.png --model tripo-v3.1 -p pbr=true -p texture_quality=detailed`. Failed jobs aren't charged.

What Tripo doesn't do here is the room. Walls, floor and ceiling are built from depth in the next step. Image-to-3D is for the things you can walk around.

If you want to try it:

* [Tripo API documentation](https://developers.tripo3d.ai/en/docs)
* [Quick start](https://developers.tripo3d.ai/en/docs/quick-start) (get a key, first request)
* [Image to 3D, H series](https://developers.tripo3d.ai/en/docs/generation-image-to-model/standard) (the call above)
* [Image to 3D, P series](https://developers.tripo3d.ai/en/docs/generation-image-to-model/p) (low-poly)
* [File upload](https://developers.tripo3d.ai/en/docs/files) and [task query](https://developers.tripo3d.ai/en/docs/task-query)
* [Convert and export](https://developers.tripo3d.ai/en/docs/models-convert) (FBX, OBJ, USDZ and others)
* [Tripo CLI guide](https://developers.tripo3d.ai/en/docs/cli)

**Step 4: Build the room**

While the objects are being made, the other lane builds the room:

1. **Empty it.** ChatGPT removes every object from the reference, which leaves a picture of the bare room.
2. **Shape it.** A depth model (MoGe) estimates how far away every pixel is. The room's walls, floor and ceiling are built from that as closed geometry. There's no template, so it doesn't assume a box. The level stops at the walls of the room the picture was taken in. What the doorway shows is set into the opening as a picture, and nothing beyond it is built.
3. **Texture it.** Each surface is drawn flat from an evenly lit version of the empty-room picture, and the parts the reference never showed are filled in to match what's beside them. Because the texture is only the material, the level's own lamps do the lighting.

https://i.redd.it/k60i03dge72i1.jpeg

**Step 5: Put every object where the picture has it**

Each model is fitted to its outline and to the depth of the reference. Then room rules apply: upright, parallel to the walls, standing on something, flush against the wall it hangs on, inside the room, and not overlapping anything. Last, all the objects are judged together from the reference camera, because a model that sits perfectly on its own outline can still hide its neighbour.

Flat things on walls, like the poster and the photos, are built as flat panels with their own picture as the face. They don't need a 3D model at all.

In the current build each object covers about two thirds of its outline on average. The best ones (the rug, the bookcase, the chest in the foreground) are at about 90% or more.

**Step 6: Light it, then check it as a level**

The scene is assembled in Blender. Every lamp's strength and colour is fitted to the reference, and the bright spots in the picture become glowing fittings.

Then it's tested as a level, not as a picture. A player-sized body, 1.8 metres tall, is walked across the floor from where the camera stood. The build fails if it can't reach at least 85% of the floor a player could stand on.

It also renders views the reference never showed:

https://i.redd.it/01mluuaje72i1.jpeg

A build only counts as complete when all of its automatic checks pass. Among them: every object has a textured model, nothing floats or overlaps, nothing sticks more than 2 cm through a wall, the room is closed, and the level can be walked and is lit along the way.

**What worked**

* Looking again. 15 of the 36 objects were only found on the later passes.
* Drawing each object again in a standard view before modelling it, instead of keeping the angle of the reference. The placement step turns the model back afterwards.
* Building the room from the empty-room picture, so the walls don't carry the shadows of furniture.
* Judging all the objects together instead of one at a time.
* The walk test. It caught things the reference camera never sees, like lamps lying on the floor and a stretch that was never lit.
* Making every fix a rule in the pipeline, not a hand edit to the scene, so the next image gets it too.

**What didn't**

* Building the corridor behind the doorway. A big part of the level was being guessed from a thin strip of the picture, and the depth model first turned it into a funnel: 1.95 m wide at the door and 4.1 m wide ten metres on. The level now stops at the room, and the doorway shows the picture.
* SAM 3 kept cutting the bed out as just its bedding, however I asked. The frame, drawers and headboard belonged to nothing. There is now a step that hands leftover pieces to the object they are part of.
* A fitted colour grade over the whole picture. The score didn't move.
* A texture size limit that went by the longer side quietly shrank the wall texture from 9,827 x 545 pixels to 2,048 x 114. Every material experiment before I found it was done on blurred walls.
* Telling it by hand which objects belong together (the desk and its chair). The vision model decides that now.

**What's still off**

Over more than 40 builds in two days, the distance between the level and the reference went from 0.43 to 0.36 on the perceptual score I use (lower is closer). It's not there yet:

* The floor should be dark tread plate with crisp seams. Mine is grey and a bit lumpy.
* Objects cut off by the edge of the picture get modelled whole and then fitted too small. The wall shelf is the clearest case.
* All the limits were tuned on this one bedroom. The next test is a second image.

I'd love to hear what you think. If you've built levels from concept art, which gave you more trouble, the room or the props? And if you've used image-to-3D for a whole scene, how did you keep the models consistent with each other?
